description: I'm Samuel, a Cyprus-based mechanical engineer and cloud & DevOps engineer, competing as a solo team. I build validated Python solvers, have run a CFD study of NASA's CRM-HL aircraft model, and deploy apps on AWS and Azure. SkyShift will be a public web tool that shows SPHEREx sky images side by side over time, so anyone can quickly spot comets, asteroids, brown dwarfs and new planets shifting position between the six-monthly all-sky scans.
summary:
SkyShift is a free web app that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey into a time machine anyone can use. Type a star, asteroid or comet name, or coordinates (RA/Dec), press Play, and every SPHEREx image of that spot is fetched from NASA's IRSA archive, aligned on the sky and played as a short movie. Blink, Difference and Stack modes make moving stars, brown dwarfs and asteroids stand out, the way Pluto was found. SkyShift also uses all 102 infrared bands: per-detector co-adds, false colour, spectra and light curves built on the fly for any clicked object, and image equations. Gaia and WISE catalogues can be overlaid, quality flags shown, and any view shared or embedded by URL. Finds are saved with full provenance and exported as a reproducible dossier. Your own FITS images can be measured too, with J2000.0 positions and magnitudes calibrated on Gaia stars. 

Everything runs in the browser: no account and nothing to install, though it can be installed on any phone or computer and works offline. I validated its positions and wavelengths against Astropy and Gaia on the challenge targets; Barnard's Star's measured motion agrees with Gaia within 2%. 

SPHEREx produces more data than any one person can inspect. SkyShift lets students, volunteers and scientists explore it within hours of it reaching the archive.
details:
What it does and how it works

• SkyShift is a time machine for the SPHEREx sky. Type a star name or coordinates (decimal, sexagesimal or galactic), or click anywhere on a real SPHEREx map of the whole sky, and press Play.

• SkyShift finds every SPHEREx image covering that spot (NASA IRSA's live search, or a pre-built index of all 1.6 million images refreshed every 3 hours), reads only the pixels it needs from NASA's public SPHEREx cloud archive, decodes the FITS files in the browser, aligns them on the sky and plays them as a movie.

• Asteroids and comets: type a name such as 4 Vesta or 67P (positions from NASA JPL Horizons) or give your own table of positions; SkyShift follows the object through every SPHEREx image along its path and can stack them all along its motion (shift-and-stack) to reach faint objects, rejecting star trails and confirming a detection only when every survey pass shows it.

• Your own images: upload a FITS image and hover for J2000.0 coordinates; click an object for its centre, J2000.0 and equinox-of-date coordinates, a magnitude calibrated on the Gaia DR3 stars in the image and the nearest catalogued star, then export the measurements: the basic data for reporting a discovery. Compressed survey images such as Pan-STARRS open too, with the display tools of a desktop FITS viewer (scales, zscale, colour maps, invert, magnifier, galactic and ecliptic coordinates, pixel table), and one click shows the image aligned with SPHEREx in the Time Machine, to blink between them.

• Modes and tabs: Movie, Blink, Difference, Stack and false Colour, plus an Invert view (dark objects on a white sky, as in WiseView: black and white in every mode, true colours kept in Colour) for faint tails and movers; spectra and light curves for any clicked object; pixel-by-pixel quality flags; Gaia DR3 and CatWISE/AllWISE overlays with predicted motion tracks (including Earth's parallax); and image equations such as mean(D5,D6) − epoch(1).

• Other pages: Explore (all-sky map showing how often each spot was imaged), Chase (fast-moving nearby stars, asteroids and comets), Live (the newest SPHEREx images), Mission (survey statistics and data freshness), Sky atlas (Aladin Lite), Saved (watch list, candidates, export) and Learn (plain-language guide).

• Relevance to the challenge: SkyShift covers every point of "Planet X and SPHEREx": objects moving and changing over time, all 102 bands, per-detector co-adds, spectra on the fly, adding and subtracting images from different times, field-of-view choice, Gaia and WISE overlays, queries by coordinates in the URL and embedding, contamination flags, Astropy and Aladin, the challenge's eight resources, and the five test targets.

Benefits

• Free and instant: no account, nothing to install, works on any phone or computer; it can also be installed as an app and works offline.

• Always fresh: new SPHEREx data appear within hours of NASA's release, even when IRSA's search service is down (SkyShift then reads the archive's storage directly).

• Light on data: about 0.24 MB per image instead of a 65 MB file (270 times less).

• Trustworthy: every frame shows its source and release; detections are labelled "candidate"; finds export as a reproducible dossier (HTML, PDF, ZIP with FITS) or as CSV, JSON or MPC ADES.

• Shareable: every view has a link, can be queried by RA/Dec in the URL and embedded in other pages.

• Resilient: runs from GitHub Pages with an independent backup on Cloudflare; installed copies keep working if a host is down.

Intended impact

SPHEREx images the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared bands, far more than any one person can inspect. SkyShift lets students, teachers, citizen scientists and researchers explore that data within hours of its release, spot moving and changing objects the way Pluto and many brown dwarfs were found, and pass well-documented candidates on for follow-up. The five challenge targets double as ready-made classroom activities.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

• Languages: JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the app; Node.js for the build and data-refresh scripts; Python with Astropy for validation.

• Web platform: Web Workers, a service worker (install, offline use, update pop-ups) and IndexedDB; no framework, so the app stays small and fast.

• Data and libraries: NASA IRSA (SPHEREx images, search, all-sky maps, WISE catalogues and images), Gaia DR3 at MAST, NEOSSat at CADC, CSA open data, WiseView links, NASA JPL Horizons (asteroid and comet positions); Aladin Lite for the sky atlas.

• Testing and hosting: Node tests and Playwright browser tests; GitHub Actions for checks and the 6-hourly refresh; GitHub Pages with a Cloudflare Pages backup.

• Hardware: a standard laptop; no special hardware is needed to build or use SkyShift.

How it is creative

• It treats the sky as a film rather than a single picture: one search becomes a movie of every SPHEREx image of that spot since the survey began.

• It uses all 102 colours: each image is tinted by its true wavelength, detectors are combined separately, and users can write their own image equations.

• The whole-sky map glows where SPHEREx has looked most often, and hovering shows how many times a spot was imaged.

• The science processing (decoding SPHEREx images, sky coordinates, wavelength tables, alignment and measurements) runs in the visitor's browser; the relay only gathers the bytes needed and unpacks the small quality-flag window.

Factors considered

• Accuracy: browser coordinates and wavelengths match Astropy to 4×10⁻¹⁰ arcsec and 10⁻¹⁵ µm on real SPHEREx files; Barnard's Star's measured motion agrees with Gaia within 2%; a faint asteroid, (500) Selinur, is detected in all six bands when its exposures are stacked; limits are stated honestly (e.g. WISE 0855 and comet 67P are too faint for SPHEREx).

• Data rules: the challenge's eight resources and pages reached from them, plus NASA JPL Horizons for asteroid and comet positions, with credits and licences.

• Accessibility: any screen size (in the Time Machine the image and all its controls fit on the screen together, from small laptops to phones), keyboard shortcuts, screen-reader labels, colour-blind-safe palette, reduced-motion and light/dark options, and every page and tab in English, Greek, Spanish and French.

• Privacy and safety: no accounts, tracking or analytics; saved work stays on the device; equations run safely (no code execution); uploads are parsed with strict limits.

• Speed and cost: small files, caching, parallel reads and a relay that collects each image's pixels in one request keep it fast; the challenge targets and fastest stars open in a few seconds from frames prepared in advance, and any other field shows its first image in about 4 seconds; static hosting keeps running costs at zero.
